column4: The deceived human is confronted with the exact workshop sequence: God created him, then straightened and balanced him, فَسَوَّىٰكَ فَعَدَلَكَ.
God is the maker who أَحْسَنَ every thing He created; this directly states the section's sense of ahsana as finishing created work well.
Moving mountains are called صُنْعَ ٱللَّهِ, the workmanship of God who perfected every thing; it makes divine creation an inspected, exact craft.
God created every thing and فَقَدَّرَهُۥ تَقْدِيرًا, measured it with exact measure, matching khalq as measuring material before the cut.
The paired verbs خَلَقَ فَسَوَّىٰ present creation as making and then bringing the workpiece into sound proportion.
The Maker measures and then guides, وَٱلَّذِى قَدَّرَ فَهَدَىٰ, so exact sizing is joined to fitness for purpose.
Every created thing is made بِقَدَرٍ, giving the section's workshop measure a universal formulation.
After creating heaven and earth, God forms people and makes their forms good, فَأَحْسَنَ صُوَرَكُمْ; workmanship and beauty are expressly joined.
Earth as a settled floor and heaven as a structure frame the statement that God formed people and perfected their forms.
This continues 82:7 by saying that the Maker assembled the human in whatever form He willed, identifying form as deliberate composition.
The Book's verses are أُحْكِمَتْ, made firm and then detailed, the section's explicit Quranic instance of work secured against defect.
The seven-layered creation contains no disparity, and the viewer is told to return the gaze to seek a crack; divine work withstands fault inspection.
The gaze is returned twice yet comes back defeated and weary, completing 67:3's inspection of a product in which no flaw can be found.
Moses names the Lord as the one who gave each thing its created form and then guided it, joining construction to intended function.
The names Creator, Originator, and Fashioner occur together, distinguishing the maker's stages that the section unfolds as one workshop.
Successive fetal materials become bones clothed with flesh and then another creation; أَحْسَنُ ٱلْخَـٰلِقِينَ praises the maker after the whole process.
From a drop God creates the human and then measures him, خَلَقَهُۥ فَقَدَّرَهُۥ, directly pairing creation with sizing.
After the embryo is held until a known term, God says فَقَدَرْنَا فَنِعْمَ ٱلْقَـٰدِرُونَ, praising the exactness of the measure.
People are made in their mothers' wombs as creation after creation in three darknesses, revealing the hidden staged workshop behind the finished human.
God forms people in the wombs however He wills, making the hidden human form a deliberate product rather than an unexplained appearance.
God proportions the human, breathes spirit, and installs hearing, sight, and hearts, continuing 32:7's good workmanship into functional completion.
God says He will proportion the clay human, breathe into him, and command prostration; the honored human follows the Maker's finishing act.
The clay human is first سَوَّيْتُهُ, brought into proportion, and then given spirit, again staging form before completed life.
God rebukes Iblis for refusing the one خَلَقْتُ بِيَدَىَّ; the wording puts the human's singular workmanship at the center of his dignity.
The drop becomes a clot, then God creates and proportions it, فَخَلَقَ فَسَوَّىٰ, compressing the workshop sequence into two verbs.
The believing companion recalls that God made the man from dust and a drop and then سَوَّىٰكَ رَجُلًا, finished him as a man.
Dust, drop, clot, childhood, maturity, and old age are one divinely managed production and decline sequence, illuminating both best form and its later reversal.
The fetus passes through formed and unformed flesh, while some humans are returned to the most decrepit age; the same ayah holds formation and deterioration together.
Some people are يُرَدُّ إِلَىٰ أَرْذَلِ ٱلْعُمُرِ, returned to the most abject age, a direct parallel to the finely made human being returned low.
Whomever God grants long life He reverses in creation, نُنَكِّسْهُ فِى ٱلْخَلْقِ, making aging an inversion of the original workmanship.
God makes weakness, then strength, then weakness and gray hair; the finished human product visibly passes back through loss of strength.
God can reassemble even the fingertips, making the finest bodily detail evidence of the Maker's exact construction and restorative power.
The scattered bones are raised and clothed with flesh before the observer's eyes, staging the damaged human body's skilled reconstruction.
Moses is set on a course so that he may be made عَلَىٰ عَيْنِى, under God's eye, a close parallel to workmanship carried out with personal care.
God tells Moses وَٱصْطَنَعْتُكَ لِنَفْسِى, “I fashioned you for Myself,” making a person both a crafted work and a work made for a purpose.
David is told to make full coats of mail, measure the links, and do sound work; craft, exact measure, and صَـٰلِحًا converge in one workshop command.
Metal heated to make ornaments or tools throws off dross, while what benefits people remains; useful finished work is separated from rejected waste.
The revealed Book is praised because no crookedness, عِوَجًا, was put in it, the textual counterpart to a shaft straightened without defect.
قَيِّمًا continues 18:1: the Book is not merely free of crookedness but set upright, like the workpiece after takwim.
The Arabic Quran is described as غَيْرَ ذِى عِوَجٍ, an artifact of speech without crookedness that calls its hearers to guard themselves.
The Quran guides to that which is أَقْوَمُ, most upright; the q-w-m family transfers the section's straightness from a made shaft to a human course.
The addressee is told to set his face upright to the fitrah on which God fashioned people, with no altering God's creation; form and right alignment coincide.
Full measure and the straight balance, ٱلْقِسْطَاسِ ٱلْمُسْتَقِيمِ, give a moral scene of exact measuring joined to straightness.
The command to give full measure and not diminish others turns accurate sizing into sound human work rather than a spoiled product.
Weighing with the straight balance, ٱلْقِسْطَاسِ ٱلْمُسْتَقِيمِ, supplies the straight measuring tool for 26:181's command.
The measuring commands culminate in a ban on depriving people and spreading corruption, explicitly placing just work against fasad.
Full measure and weight are commanded, and corruption after the earth's repair is forbidden; exact work stands directly between islah and fasad.
God raises the heaven and sets the balance, pairing cosmic construction with the standard by which things are kept proportionate.
Humans are forbidden to upset the balance established in 55:7, defining a boundary against spoiling the Maker's measure.
The command to establish weight justly and not diminish the balance makes exact measure an entrusted human imitation of ordered making.
Allah does not make sound عَمَلَ ٱلْمُفْسِدِينَ, the work of corrupters; amal, islah, and fasad meet in a single verdict on defective work.
God distinguishes the corrupter from the reformer, ٱلْمُفْسِدَ مِنَ ٱلْمُصْلِحِ, stating the precise lexical boundary behind salihat as sound, unreduced work.
Those who believe and do sound deeds have their evils removed and their condition repaired, وَأَصْلَحَ بَالَهُمْ; good work is answered by divine repair.
Believers are commanded to speak a straight, sound word, قَوْلًا سَدِيدًا, the human verbal counterpart to a straightened workpiece.
God promises in response to 33:70 to يُصْلِحْ لَكُمْ أَعْمَـٰلَكُمْ, repair their deeds, directly treating human outputs as corrigible work.
Those who believe and do sound deeds are set against corrupters on earth; righteous work and fasad are denied equal treatment.
Evildoers cannot be made equal in life and death to believers who do sound deeds; سَآءَ مَا يَحْكُمُونَ condemns that as defective judgment.
God says وَأَصْلَحْنَا لَهُۥ زَوْجَهُۥ, that He repaired Zechariah's wife for him, a Quranic instance of divine islah applied to a human body.
The full exception returns outside surah 95: believers who do sound deeds receive أَجْرٌ غَيْرُ مَمْنُونٍ, an unbroken reward for sound work.
Belief and sound deeds again lead to أَجْرٌ غَيْرُ مَمْنُونٍ, confirming that the lasting wage belongs to work that remains sound.
The Prophet is promised أَجْرًا غَيْرَ مَمْنُونٍ, the same uncut reward that counters the section's dictionary image of a crookedly healed wage.
Humanity is declared in loss, providing the same universal fall from a privileged human condition that surah 95 then qualifies by exception.
The loss of 103:2 excludes those who believe and do sound deeds, closely matching the structural and verbal rescue in 95:6.
God does not waste the reward of one who أَحْسَنَ عَمَلًا; excellent workmanship, human work, and an undamaged wage meet in one sentence.
What people possess runs out while what is with God remains, and the patient are paid by the best they did; passing product and lasting wage are joined.
Whoever does عَمِلَ صَـٰلِحًا in faith receives a good life and reward by the best of their work, uniting all three workshop terms.
Life and death are created to test which person is أَحْسَنُ عَمَلًا, shifting excellence from God's workmanship to the quality of human work.
After mentioning God's creation of heavens and earth, the ayah says the test is which person is best in work, linking Maker and tested makers.
Those who hold fast to the Book and establish prayer are called reformers, and God does not waste أَجْرَ ٱلْمُصْلِحِينَ.
ٱلْبَـٰقِيَـٰتُ ٱلصَّـٰلِحَـٰتُ are the sound deeds that remain and are better in reward, directly naming durable work.
The lasting sound deeds are better with the Lord in reward and return, again identifying salihat as the work that survives.
God answers that He never lets the work of any worker be lost, عَمَلَ عَـٰمِلٍ, sharpening the section's play between the working part and enduring human work.
Iron is softened for David before the measured armor-making command of 34:11, supplying the workable material on the divine craftsman's bench.
Dhu al-Qarnayn levels iron blocks between two sides, heats them to fire, and pours molten metal over them: a fully staged process of making sound work.
The completed barrier cannot be climbed or pierced, so 18:96's careful process is vindicated by a product fit for its purpose.
Allah has created both the people and what they make, وَمَا تَعْمَلُونَ, putting human makers and their products inside the greater Maker's work.
Jesus shapes from clay the form of a bird and it becomes living by God's permission; khalq visibly retains its sense of measured forming.
God recalls Jesus forming a bird-shape from clay by permission, again separating skilled form-making from God's gift of life.
“We created you; why do you not affirm?” makes the finished human the evidence placed before the skeptical addressee.
The hearers are made to inspect the reproductive material they emit, beginning the maker-versus-material inquiry continued in 56:59.
The question asks whether people create the emitted material's human result or God does, locating true workmanship beyond the visible makers.
“Would the one who created not know?” reasons from the maker's intimate knowledge of the made thing, the stance assumed by the workshop image.
Noah addresses God as أَحْكَمُ ٱلْحَـٰكِمِينَ, the exact divine superlative behind 95:8 in an appeal for sound judgment.
“Who is better than Allah in judgment?” gives the direct rhetorical parallel to asking whether Allah is the wisest or firmest of judges.
The sky is built, adorned, and found to have no fissures; beauty and structural soundness are one inspected piece of workmanship.
God knows what every womb bears, what it lacks or increases, and every thing with Him is by measure; hidden formation is governed by exact sizing.
God places stabilizers and blessings in the earth and measures its sustenance in four days, making provision another deliberately measured work.
The one who produced the bones the first time will revive them; first manufacture is the warrant for repairing the decayed product.
Divining arrows are called an abomination مِنْ عَمَلِ ٱلشَّيْطَـٰنِ; the carefully made arrow becomes the opposite of salih work through corrupt use.
Seeking decisions by divining arrows is forbidden; the section's smoothed arrow is here bounded by an illicit purpose rather than faulty manufacture.
Satan promises to command people to alter God's creation, making deformation of the Maker's finished work an explicit transgression.
One walking fallen on his face is opposed to one walking سَوِيًّا on a straight path, bodily abasement against upright human alignment.
The question introduces those greatest in loss with respect to their works, preparing an inspection of output that fails despite effort.
Their effort is lost while they think they يُحْسِنُونَ صُنْعًا, are perfecting workmanship; apparent good craft can be radically misjudged.
Their works collapse and receive no weight on Judgment Day, the rejected product of 18:104 failing even the final measure.
What worldly workers manufactured is void in the Hereafter and what they did is false, a direct picture of output that cannot remain.
God turns the deeds of the deniers into scattered dust, the fate of work that proves wholly unsound at inspection.
The punished faces are عَامِلَةٌ نَّاصِبَةٌ, laboring and exhausted; effort alone has produced no sound or saving work.
Those invoked besides God cannot create even a fly, exposing the absolute limit of rival makers against the craftsmanship attributed to God.
After “this is God's creation,” challengers are told to show what others created, turning workmanship into visible evidence against false partners.
The invoked beings create nothing and are themselves created, reversing maker and artifact to expose false claims of agency.
The idolaters are challenged to show what their partners created of the earth, demanding an actual product rather than a claimed maker.
The spider's house is the frailest of houses; it supplies a natural image of construction that exists yet fails as reliable shelter.
The flawless barrier of 18:96–97 will be leveled when God's promise comes, setting a boundary even on excellent human workmanship.
Iblis answers 38:75 by judging fire superior to clay, reducing the honored crafted human to raw material and ignoring the Maker's finishing work.
“Humanity was created weak” places constitutional weakness beside the best conformation, preventing good workmanship from being mistaken for self-sufficiency.
The human is said to have been created anxious and grasping, a moral susceptibility set against the body's best conformation.
The praying are excepted from 70:19's created restlessness, paralleling the faithful workers excepted from humanity's downward course in surah 95.
Bad and good are declared unequal even when the abundance of the bad impresses; quantity cannot turn defective output into sound work.
Abraham asks whether people worship what they carve; the artisan's product becomes an object of worship instead of evidence of its maker.
False partners are asked whether they created something like God's creation so the products became confused, testing maker-claims by comparable workmanship.
The one who creates is denied equality with one who does not, a concise boundary between the true Maker and a claimed one.
This identifies the addressee of 82:7 as the human deceived about his generous Lord, so the workmanship is presented as grounds against ingratitude.
The human workpiece begins as an extract of clay, supplying the first material for the staged construction completed in 23:14.
The drop is placed in a secure lodging, a controlled intermediate step between selected material and the transformed body of 23:14.
The human starts as an emitted drop, establishing the unpromising raw material that 75:38 says God creates and proportions.
The Maker finishes the sequence by producing the male and female pair, showing that proportioning in 75:38 includes differentiated human form.
The question points to humanity's creation from a humble fluid, opening the measured production sequence that ends at 77:23.
The material is put in a secure receptacle, an intermediate placement that makes the womb part of an ordered production process.
The embryo remains until a known measure or term, إِلَىٰ قَدَرٍ مَّعْلُومٍ, supplying the exact limit praised in 77:23.
God announces the clay material from which He will create a human, setting up the proportioning and enlivening in 15:29.
The announced creation of a human from clay supplies the raw material before the explicit proportioning in 38:72.
Human progeny is made from an extract of humble fluid, the material stage between 32:7's universal craftsmanship and 32:9's finishing.
The oath by the soul and the One who proportioned it extends divine taswiya from the visible body to the inward human self.
The proportioned soul of 91:7 is then shown both corruption and reverence, explaining why a well-made human can yield sound or spoiled work.
People are reminded that God created them in stages, a compact statement of the successive workmanship elsewhere shown in the womb.
The human is created from a mixed drop for testing and then made hearing and seeing, joining raw material, purpose, and fitted faculties.
The Lord creates the human from a clinging clot, a terse material image that makes the refined human's origin visible.
The human is commanded to look at what he was created from, turning bodily origin into an inspection of the Maker's work.
The gushing fluid supplies the answer to 86:5 and the raw material from which the human form is made.
God's making of two eyes identifies a paired, functional detail in the carefully equipped human body.
A tongue and two lips continue the inventory of fitted human parts, showing completion for speech rather than form alone.
After fitting the organs, God guides the human to two paths; made capacities carry a moral purpose and choice.
God brings people from the womb knowing nothing and equips hearing, sight, and hearts, a functional completion intended to produce gratitude.
God brings people into being and makes hearing, sight, and hearts, another inventory of faculties fitted into the human product.
The children of Adam are honored and preferred over much of creation, supplying the elevated valuation from which being returned low becomes a fall.
God says He created and then formed humanity before the command to prostrate, joining human making to bestowed rank.
Dhu al-Qarnayn asks for strength to make a barrier, identifying purpose, labor, and intended function before the material process of 18:96.
Noah is commanded to manufacture the Ark under God's eyes and revelation, a created object made under explicit divine oversight.
The repeated Ark command, “make under Our eyes,” reinforces the image of careful manufacture supervised by its true designer.
God teaches David the manufacture of armor that protects people, a concrete case of skilled work made sound by fitness for purpose.
“Were they created from nothing, or are they the creators?” forces humans to distinguish product from maker.
The challenge expands from human self-creation to the making of heavens and earth, exposing the absence of any rival workshop.
The heavens are completed as seven in two days, each assigned its command and the lower one adorned and guarded; construction includes order and finish.
The earth is spread, stabilized, and made to grow every kind of thing in measured balance, مِن كُلِّ شَىْءٍ مَّوْزُونٍ.
God has made for every thing a measure, قَدْرًا, generalizing the limits and exact sizing visible in the workshop image.
Water is sent down in due measure and lodged in the earth, showing provision handled by the same deliberate measure as created form.
God denies weariness in the first creation and points to a new creation, treating remaking as no defect or exhaustion in the Maker.
The disputing human forgets that God created him from a drop, setting up the decayed-bone challenge answered by 36:79.
The human displays rotten bones and asks who can revive them, presenting the apparently ruined product whose Maker is named in 36:79.
Death is measured out among people and the Maker is not to be outstripped, establishing control over the finished body's end.
God can replace people with their likes and produce them in a form they do not know, extending workmanship beyond the present form.
Knowledge of the first creation is invoked as the reason to recognize the possibility of the further making in 56:61.
The Quran's lack of many inconsistencies is offered as evidence of its divine source, another fault inspection of a firmly made text.
God sends down the best discourse as a mutually consistent, repeated Book; excellence here includes coherence throughout the completed work.
Some verses of the Book are مُّحْكَمَـٰتٌ and form its foundation, using the root the section explains as secured against defect or doubt.
After satanic interference is removed, God يُحْكِمُ ءَايَـٰتِهِۦ, makes His signs firm, giving the root an active textual repair context.
The Book is declared to contain no doubt, matching the section's dictionary statement that what is muhkam admits no uncertainty.
The Quran cannot be fabricated, confirms what precedes it, and details the Book without doubt from the Lord: sound provenance and sound construction coincide.
Falsehood cannot reach the revelation from before or behind, making the Book a secured work protected from corrupting intrusion.
Shuayb's address names his people's measuring and commercial work before commanding its repair in the following ayat.
Full measure and weight are commanded and فساد in the earth forbidden, directly opposing accurate work to corruption.
Shuayb says he desires only reform as far as he can, naming islah as the purpose behind correcting the defective measures.
When forbidden to spread corruption, the people claim they are only reformers; the false label tests what counts as genuinely sound work.
God identifies those self-named reformers as the actual corrupters, policing the section's lexical boundary between islah and fasad.
Moses commands Aaron to set matters right and not follow the path of corrupters, making reform the active alternative to spoiled communal work.
The mature believer asks God to make his descendants sound for him, extending divine islah across human generations.
The Prophet is commanded فَٱسْتَقِمْ كَمَآ أُمِرْتَ, to be straight as ordered, turning the artisan's straightening into a human stance.
The call to religion includes “be straight as you were commanded,” another direct moral use of the section's line-straightness.
Those who say their Lord is Allah and then remain straight receive angelic assurance, showing what a human life held to its line yields.
Those who affirm their Lord and then remain straight are freed from fear and grief, the parallel outcome of moral straightening.
Every hardship and step is recorded as a sound deed, because God does not waste the reward of those who do well.
Patience is joined to the assurance that God does not waste the reward of the muhsinin, preserving the return on well-done work.
Joseph's secure establishment in the land is followed by the maxim that God does not waste the reward of those who do well.
Joseph links reverence and patience to the rule that God does not waste the reward of the muhsinin, again protecting good work's wage.
The patient are paid their reward without reckoning, another formulation of a wage not clipped or exhausted.
God repays those who do evil for what they did and rewards those who do well with the best, judging outputs by their quality.
Believers who do sound deeds have faults removed and are rewarded according to the best they used to do.
Good deeds remove bad deeds, treating sound human acts as work whose effect repairs earlier damage.
For the repentant believer who does sound work, God changes bad deeds into good ones, a moral refashioning of spoiled output.
One who pardons and repairs has his reward with God; islah and ajr are explicitly joined.
Game coming within reach of hands and spears supplies the Quranic setting for the very spear whose shaft the section imagines an artisan straightening.
Animal hides become light tents for travel and encampment, showing the section's measured leather as material made into a fit human object.
The blessed receive a gift غَيْرَ مَجْذُوذٍ, not cut off, a nonlexical parallel to the unbroken wage of sound work.
Good speech ascends and sound work raises it, giving صالح work a direction and durability that corrupt output lacks.
Some believers have mixed a sound deed with another bad one, presenting human output as a composite whose quality requires repair.
A believer who does sound deeds has his striving neither denied nor lost, and it is written down, securing the work's lasting account.
God removes the worst of what believers did and rewards them by the best of their work, preserving the well-made part rather than the defect.
God commands that judgments between people be made with justice, anchoring the h-k-m root's craftsmanship metaphor in its governing sense.
Shuayb asks God to decide truthfully and calls Him the best of judges, a contextual parallel to surah 95's closing question.
The Prophet is told to wait until God judges, for He is the best of judges; the title marks the reliability of the final verdict.
Jacob is called the best of judges when the brothers resolve to await his permission or God's judgment.
The plea “My Lord, judge with truth” identifies truthful adjudication as the governing sense alongside the section's firmness sense.
God asks whether those who submit should be treated like criminals, posing the just discrimination that must govern the evaluation of human work.
“How do you judge?” rebukes the leveling rejected in 68:35 and echoes the rhetorical challenge of 95:8.
The verb سَاهَمَ describes casting lots aboard Jonah's ship; it may preserve the lot-arrow scene, though the ayah does not itself name an arrow.
Night worship is said to be أَقْوَمُ قِيلًا, more upright in speech; the q-w-m link is exact, but its relation to bodily workmanship is indirect.
The question asks whether humans are harder to create than heaven and immediately says that God built it, turning creation into an explicit construction comparison.
God raises the heaven's canopy and proportions it, فَسَوَّىٰهَا, so the building announced in 79:27 ends in exact alignment.
The human is made from dry ringing clay like pottery, bringing raw material and fashioned artifact together more explicitly than a generic creation statement.
Earth's adornment is itself made as a test of who is أَحْسَنُ عَمَلًا, joining a beautified product to the quality of human workmanship.
The best speech is attributed to one who calls to God and does sound work, combining the section's ahsan and salih language in a human output.
People are forbidden to corrupt the earth after its repair, بَعْدَ إِصْلَـٰحِهَا, stating the section's islah–fasad boundary as a temporal reversal.
The transgressing leaders are those who corrupt the earth and do not repair it, pairing both sides of the lexical opposition in one description.
Reforming relations between people is one of the few kinds of private counsel praised, and doing it for God is promised a great reward; islah and ajr meet.
Exact scales are set for Judgment so no soul is wronged and even a mustard-seed weight is brought, applying flawless measure to the assessment of work.
The Book and balance establish justice, while iron supplies strength and human benefits; measure, judgment, and craft material converge in one divine provision.
Full measure and weight in justice are commanded without overburdening a soul, another direct formulation of straight, proportionate human work.
A good word is likened to a good tree with a firm root and high branch, giving sound output a structure that stands.
The sound tree continually yields fruit by its Lord's permission, completing 14:24's image of work whose goodness remains productive.
A bad word is an uprooted bad tree with no stability, a concrete reversal of the straightened, sound product.
Believers who do sound deeds are called the best of created beings, joining human workmanship to the final quality assigned to the human creature.
The best creatures of 98:7 receive lasting gardens as their reward, so sound work again yields an enduring wage.
The deliberate killing anticipated by the spear test requires a livestock equivalent judged by two just people, adding exact equivalence and judgment to 5:94's spear scene.
Thamud skillfully carve houses from mountains yet are warned not to spread corruption, placing impressive workmanship directly beside fasad.
The jinn make buildings, images, basins, and fixed cauldrons for Solomon, and David's family is commanded to work gratefully; product and amal share one workshop.
Corruption appears on land and sea through what human hands have earned; spoiled worldly conditions are treated as the product of human work.
The defrauders demand full measure when receiving from others, showing a measuring practice corrupted by self-interest.
When those same people measure or weigh for others they diminish, making defective measure the deliberate opposite of sound workmanship.
God says He built the heaven with might, supplying another direct cosmic construction scene for divine craftsmanship.
God spreads the earth and calls Himself an excellent spreader, so the construction of 51:47 is complemented by a fitted floor.
After making what is on earth for people, God turns to heaven and proportions seven heavens, extending taswiya to a layered structure.
Heaven is still smoke when God commands heaven and earth to come willingly, supplying the unformed material and obedience before 41:12's completion.
People are told to inspect how the camel was created, an invitation to infer the maker's workmanship from a finished creature.
The same inspection asks how heaven was raised, shifting from creature to large-scale construction.
The mountains are inspected for how they were set, adding stable placement to the sequence of created forms.
The earth is inspected for how it was spread, completing the ordered environment in which the creature stands.
God creates the male and female pair, identifying differentiated human forms as products of one Maker.
The pair of 53:45 is made from an emitted drop, revealing the modest material beneath the differentiated finished forms.
God's creation of the human opens a two-step statement whose next ayah supplies a fitted human capacity.
Teaching the created human articulate expression shows the product completed with a distinctive working faculty.
God brings people forth and makes hearing, sight, and hearts for them, another functional inventory of the finished human.
Human creation from ringing clay and molded mud identifies the raw substance that is later proportioned and enlivened.
The objectors ask whether bones and crumbled remains can become a new creation, presenting the human product after apparent total failure.
They are told to become stone or iron, carrying 17:49's challenge to materials that seem still harder to restore to life.
Asked who will return them, the answer is the One who originated them the first time; first workmanship guarantees reconstruction.
The human asks whether he will be brought out alive after death, voicing the objection that a ruined product cannot be remade.
God answers by reminding the human that He created him before when he was nothing, making original manufacture the proof of repair.
People are asked whether they see how God begins creation and then repeats it, presenting making and remaking as one competence.
Travel through the earth is commanded to inspect how creation began, after which God produces the later creation.
God begins creation and then repeats it before people return to Him, another concise cycle of making and remaking.
Beginning and repeating creation belong to God, and repetition is described as easiest for Him, denying difficulty in reconstructing the work.
God promises to repeat creation just as He began it, explicitly treating the future body as a renewed first work.
God is the One who begins and repeats, a compressed formulation of the Maker's power to reproduce His work.
The Creator of heaven and earth did not tire in making them and is able to revive the dead, joining faultless first work to human restoration.
The six-stage creation of heaven, earth, and what lies between caused God no weariness, excluding fatigue from the divine workshop.
Cattle are described as created for humans from what God's hands made, giving another direct divine-hand formulation for useful products.
Molten copper is made to flow for Solomon and jinn labor under divine command, supplying material and workforce for the products listed in 34:13.
A people identify Gog and Magog as corrupters and offer payment for a barrier, stating the defect and proposed wage before the sound construction begins.
Thamud carve houses from mountains with great skill, yet the surrounding rebuke makes virtuoso craft insufficient without sound conduct.
Thamud carve mountain houses feeling secure, a durable-looking human product whose security does not survive moral corruption.
Thamud cut rock in the valley, a repeated Quranic glimpse of forceful, skilled shaping of resistant material.
Elijah asks whether his people abandon أَحْسَنَ ٱلْخَـٰلِقِينَ for Baal, applying the maker superlative in a direct worship contrast.
Nine men in the city spread corruption and do not repair, another explicit pairing of fasad with the absence of islah.
God's treasuries contain all things, but He sends them down only by a known measure; provisioning follows exact limits rather than accident.
Water is sent from the sky by measure and revives dead land, making calibrated provision productive and restorative.
Provision is sent down by measure because unlimited abundance would provoke transgression, showing measure fitted to the recipient's condition.
God appoints phases for the moon so years and reckoning can be known, making measured form serve a precise human function.
The sun and moon run by exact calculation, a cosmic parallel to the measured, dependable working part.
God measures the moon through stages until it resembles an old palm stalk, displaying form governed through a sequence of exact measures.
The Prophet is guided to a straight path and an upright religion, transferring the section's physical straightness into an ordered life.

Holding firmly to revelation is joined to being on a straight path, making the sound Book the means of maintaining human alignment.
God's straight path is to be followed rather than branching paths, a line image that clarifies what it means for a life to stay straightened.
Believers ask for a surah, but when a decisive or firmly established surah is sent the sick-hearted recoil; muhkam textual form tests its hearers.
David and Solomon judge the damaged field, beginning a passage in which divine hukm is followed by David's taught manufacture of armor.
Solomon is given understanding of the case and both prophets receive judgment and knowledge, bridging adjudication to the craft instruction in 21:80.
God says He created the human and knows the soul's whisper, applying the maker's intimate knowledge to the interior of the product.

Iblis asks whether he should prostrate to one God created from clay, again treating material as grounds to reject the finished work.

Pharaoh commands clay to be fired and a tower built to challenge Moses' God, a carefully made artifact serving arrogant falsehood.
Pharaoh commands Haman to build him a lofty structure, repeating the scene of corrupt authority directing human workmanship.
The tower's stated purpose is to reach the heavenly ways and inspect Moses' God, exposing the false aim assigned to the construction.
Fortified houses fail their owners and are ruined by their own hands and believers' hands, a dramatic unmaking of trusted human workmanship.
